name: Pedro Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a big hydraulic excavator at an open-pit lithium mine, loading ore into haul trucks. It's a 250-tonne machine, and on a good day I'll load sixty trucks without one of them waiting. I start at six, do my pre-start checks, walk around the machine with a torch looking for leaks, and then it's digging until the lunch break. What I like is getting a clean, flat floor and a straight face by the end of the shift, so the next operator has an easy start.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's your role beyond the machine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the apprentice program for the mobile plant operators, which I set up eleven years ago. I take on two or three young ones a year and teach them the way my uncle taught me on a backhoe when I was sixteen. Outside work, my wife Marisol and I have a small cattle block about forty minutes from town, eighty head. That's my weekends, and where I'll spend my retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise about nothing much. Good tools for the office, maybe, but the pit still needs operators. I'd say it at work and maybe in the stock agents' group chat I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be pleased. I like things the way they are. I've got about four years to go, and I'd like to finish them in the seat and hand my apprentices over to someone good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to check cattle prices and the weather for the block, and I'd keep doing that. I'd keep running the apprentice program and work towards retiring at sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the apprentice program matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how I learned, from a man who took the time. Nobody gets good from a video or a simulator alone. You learn by sitting next to someone who's done it for thirty years and having them tell you, gently, that you're doing it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which apprentice are you proudest of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A young woman called Hana, from three years ago. She came in nervous, now she's one of the best loaders on site. She sends me a photo of her machine every time she gets a new one.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of noise about not much, good for the office maybe, but the pit still needs operators. I'd say it at work and in the stock agents' group chat.
S0.think: Privately I'd be pleased, because I like things as they are. I'd finish my last four years in the seat and hand my apprentices to someone good.
S0.do: Carries on as now, using an AI app now and then for cattle prices and weather. Keeps running the apprentice program and works towards retiring at 62.
S0.quote: Nobody gets good from a video or a simulator alone.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro's identity rests on teaching: his apprentice program is his legacy. His cattle block gives him a second life to retire into, which makes him secure. He uses AI casually and without fuss, for farm-related things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of mining, always has been. When I started we had cable shovels and no GPS. I'd tell the young ones to learn the new gear and not complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's manageable for me. I'd probably finish my time without much trouble. What worries me is whether the company keeps taking on apprentices if fewer operators are needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new systems once the first few operators had them working, because I'd want to teach them properly. I'd push management to keep the apprentice intake going, maybe retraining it towards the new machines. And I'd keep putting money into the cattle block, maybe another few head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to management about apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them if they stop training young people now, they'll have nobody who understands the machines in ten years. Companies should be training their own people, not waiting for the government to do it. That's their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let AI help you teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, once I'd seen it work. The simulator they bought is all right for the basics. But the real teaching happens in the cab, with the dirt and the noise and the boss on the radio.

S1.say: I'd say change has always been part of mining, since we started with cable shovels and no GPS. I'd tell the young ones to learn the new gear and not complain.
S1.think: Privately it's manageable and I'd likely finish my time without trouble. What worries me is whether the company keeps taking on apprentices if fewer operators are needed.
S1.do: Learns new systems once others have them working so he can teach them properly. Pushes management to keep the apprentice intake going, and adds a few head of cattle to the block.
S1.quote: Companies should be training their own people, not waiting for the government to do it.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro sees training as the company's duty, not the state's, which fits his traditional outlook. He would learn new systems only after they proved themselves, then teach them. His worry is the apprentice pipeline rather than himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast for anybody. Businesses would be rushing, families would be caught out. I'd say people need to look after their own and lean on their families, because the government won't be ready either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'm all right, I'd be sixty with the block and our savings. What bothers me is the apprentices. I've told those kids there's a career in this, and in two years there might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to each of my current apprentices in the first month and help them pick a trade that would hold up, like diesel fitting or electrical. I'd probably retire within a year rather than learn a system I'd only use for a few months, and move to the block full-time. I'd grow the herd a bit and maybe give a couple of the young ones weekend work on the farm if they needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Guilty, a bit, about what I told those kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years change things for you compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I can't finish my apprentices. With five or ten, I'd see them through and set them up for the new jobs. With two, I'd be sending them off half-trained into a world I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said families should lean on each other. What would that look like for yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son's a builder, and our daughter teaches. I'd tell them if anything goes wrong, the block's there, there's room and there's work. That's what family land is for.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast for anybody, with businesses rushing and families caught out. I'd tell people to look after their own and lean on family, because the government won't be ready either.
S2.think: Privately I'm all right at sixty with the block and savings. What bothers me is the apprentices, because I've told them there's a career in this and in two years there might not be.
S2.do: Talks with each apprentice in the first month about moving into trades like diesel fitting or electrical. Retires within a year to work the cattle block full-time, grows the herd and offers young people weekend farm work.
S2.feel: Uneasy and somewhat guilty about the promises he made to his apprentices.
S2.quote: I've told those kids there's a career in this, and in two years there might not be.
S2.fieldNote: Pedro's guilt about his apprentices was the strongest emotion he showed. He looks to family and land rather than government as the safety net, consistent with his outlook. The block is his backup plan and his family's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a few years, so let's be sensible about it. Train people for the jobs that'll still be there and don't panic. I'd say it at work and to the farming families I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is fine for me. I'd be sixty-three, and I'd planned to retire at sixty-two. I'd get to finish my apprentices properly, which matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until sixty-two, and I'd learn the remote loading system once a few operators had shown it worked, so my last apprentices learn both ways. I'd push the apprentice program towards maintenance of the automated machines. On the block, I'd look at the drone and water sensor gear the other cattlemen are using, once I'd seen it on a neighbour's place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's enough time for me to do things right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can finish what I started. Every apprentice I've signed gets through, and the last group learns the new machines with me. That's the difference between leaving a mess and leaving things in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use technology on the farm. Is that a change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'll use anything once someone I trust has shown it works. My neighbour Doug's had water sensors on his tanks for two years and hasn't lost a beast to a dry trough since.

S3.say: I'd say a few years is enough to be sensible, training people for the jobs that will still exist and not panicking. I'd say it at work and among the farming families.
S3.think: Privately five years is fine, since I'd planned to retire at sixty-two. I'd get to finish my apprentices properly, which matters to me.
S3.do: Works until 62 and learns the remote loading system once others prove it, so his last apprentices learn both ways. Steers the apprentice program towards maintaining automated machines and adds sensor gear to the farm after seeing it on a neighbour's place.
S3.feel: Calm, with enough time to do things right.
S3.quote: That's the difference between leaving a mess and leaving things in order.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Pedro finish his apprentices and leave in order, which is what he cares about most. He is steady with technology, adopting it once a trusted neighbour has shown it works. He sees the farm as a place to use new tools too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who isn't ready by then hasn't been paying attention. Companies should train, families should plan. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's after I'm gone from the mine. I'd be on the block full-time. I'd just want to know the apprentice program goes on in some form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retire at sixty-two, as planned, and hand the apprentice program to Hana if she'd take it. I'd buy the neighbouring forty acres if it came up for sale, because land holds its value whatever the robots do. And I'd keep an eye on the new farm gear, but wait until it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That one feels normal to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why land, in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you can't print more of it and a robot can't take it off you. My grandfather said that, and he was right through every change I've seen. Whatever happens, you can grow food on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you advise your kids the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to hold on to the block after we're gone, not sell it. It's not about money, it's about having somewhere that's yours. They know that already.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone not ready by then hasn't been paying attention. Companies should train and families should plan.
S4.think: Privately it's after I've left the mine and I'd be on the block full-time. I'd just want the apprentice program to carry on in some form.
S4.do: Retires at 62 as planned and hands the apprentice program to Hana. Buys the neighbouring forty acres if it comes up and waits for new farm gear to be proven.
S4.feel: Calm, the picture feels normal to him.
S4.quote: You can't print more of it and a robot can't take it off you.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Pedro is fully at ease and turns his attention to land and legacy. His grandfather's saying about land captured his outlook. Handing the program to Hana, his former apprentice, would close the circle for him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be sending my apprentices off half-trained with nowhere to go. What would help is companies keeping their apprenticeships going and switching them to the new machines, not shutting them down to save money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the young ones. Everyone asks the old fellows like me, and we'll be fine. It's the nineteen-year-old who just signed up to be an operator that you should be talking to.

headlineQuote: It's the nineteen-year-old who just signed up to be an operator that you should be talking to.
portrait: Pedro Young is a 58-year-old senior excavator operator at an open-pit lithium mine who set up and runs the site's apprentice program, with a small cattle block he and his wife Marisol will retire to. He uses AI now and then for cattle prices and weather and adopts new tools once someone he trusts has shown they work. He is calm in most pictures and only uneasy in AGI by 2028, feeling guilty that he promised his apprentices a career that might vanish. He believes companies should train their own people and that family and land are the real safety net. His legacy is the young operators he has taught.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he would be sending his apprentices off half-trained with nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping their apprenticeships going and switching them to the new machines instead of shutting them down.
